purpose: Reference intake for the existing Punjab Chiefs playables, childhood-to-Lahore development, and later Ranjit Singh chapters.
status: Reference-only. Scene hooks below are proposed adaptations, not newly implemented gameplay.
review_scope: Verified file hashes; inspected title/frontmatter and selected relevant passages. This is not an exhaustive fact-check of every book.
editorial_policy: Retain legends, anecdotes, beliefs and disputed accounts as usable dramatic material.
Keep source attribution, chronology variants and adaptation decisions in production records; do not require repetitive source disclaimers in dramatic scenes.
Distinguish an author's account from original dialogue and actions designed for the game.
Repeated accounts from dependent books are not independent corroboration.
Keep observed 1838 court events and mature-empire institutions distinct from the 1792 childhood baseline.
Prescriptive texts provide characters' ideals and possible practices, not a universal uniform or rule for every Sikh household.

sources.title: Ranjit Singh and the Sikh Barrier Between Our Growing Empire and Central Asia
sources.author: Sir Lepel Griffin
sources.printing_statement: Fifth Thousand; not a numbered fifth edition
sources.source_relationship: Preface expressly reuses Griffin's The Punjab Chiefs, The Rajas of the Punjab and family/official records.

passages.account: Budha Singh's piebald mare Desi and wounded warrior tradition.
passages.use: Deepen the existing Desi recollection; shared lineage with The Punjab Chiefs.

passages.account: Maha Singh's wedding attendants cut horse fodder on a Nabha preserve; a clash during festivities produces a subsequent grievance.
passages.use: A horse-care errand that exposes territorial authority and restrained anger. This concerns Ranjit's parents, not the Nakai marriage.

passages.account: Maha Singh collapses on his elephant; the driver withdraws him, the army retreats, and he dies at Gujranwala three days later in this version.
passages.use: Evacuation and an anxious journey home; preserve alongside alternative Sodhran accounts.

passages.account: Hashmat Khan reaches the child's elephant and an attendant kills him, dated 1790 here.
passages.use: A distinct remembered rescue; do not silently fuse it with a later Hashmat encounter.

passages.account: During the Miani siege, refused appeals through Sahib Singh Bedi precede a Beas flood that sweeps through the besiegers' camp.
passages.use: Messenger work, a providential telling, rising water and an escape with animals.

passages.account: Griffin reports twelve Afghan guns lost in the flooded Jhelum and eight recovered by Ranjit; a grant of Lahore is promised in exchange.
passages.use: Survey, salvage and convoy work in the Lahore prelude; the grant story remains attributed.

passages.account: Assurances from Lahore's inhabitants precede opened gates and entry in July 1799.
passages.use: Confidential messages, approach and a change of control inside the city.

passages.account: The same book dates the Nakai marriage to 1798 in one passage and 1802 in another.
passages.use: Keep both date claims in the variant record; the delegation remains usable.

sources.title: Prem Sumarag: The Testimony of a Sanatan Sikh
sources.kind: Translation of a prescriptive rahit text with a modern scholarly introduction
sources.dating: Introduction, printed 3–7 / PDF 10–14, discusses disputed dates. The 1815 composite manuscript cited on printed 6 / PDF 13 contains chapter 1; it does not securely date all later chapters.

passages.account: Gifts include money, sugar candy, clothes, weapons and a sword-belt; gifts for the groom's mother include clothes, coconut and bangles. Expenditure is tied to resources.
passages.use: Visible packing and spending decisions in the Nakai delegation; selecting these wedding prescriptions for a betrothal visit is an adaptation.

passages.account: Preparation includes grain sorting and washing, a clean pot and surface, seasoning in ghee, slow cooking, breads and rice.
passages.use: Work at the hearth before the exile hospitality conversation.

passages.account: The text urges feeding visitors and reserving a portion for a hungry Hindu, Muslim or Khalsa traveller, even with little available.
passages.use: An offered meal with household consequences; preserve the characters' connection between hospitality and blessing.

passages.account: Travel permits adaptation to local eating customs. A household drinking jar is kept cool and clean, with rose petals and cardamom.
passages.use: A supplied rest stop in the riding journey; do not present the ingredients as water purification.

passages.account: Prescribed attire layers a turban and optional ornaments, front-opening jama, trousers or socks, sash, sword-belt and sword.
passages.use: Status and preparation through clothing; not a universal Sikh uniform.

passages.account: A dwelling, separate cooking space, garden, tank, reception bower, stable and well are described according to resources.
passages.use: A legible warning and dependent-escort route in the revenge scene; not a reconstruction of Dal Singh's actual house.

passages.account: Washing, recitation and morning devotion precede work; limited washing is allowed where bathing is impracticable.
passages.use: A later storytelling frame with water gathering and distant singing; not proof of the earlier Bahrwal legend's actual setting.

passages.account: Camp enclosure, pioneers and axe-men, four-sided watches and differentiated command posts are prescribed for an army.
passages.use: Shared perimeter work and disputed duties among allied chiefs; scale this large-army ideal to the authored scene.

sources.title: The Court and Camp of Runjeet Sing
sources.author: W. G. Osborne
sources.kind: British mission journal with introductory history, illustrations and later concluding material
sources.observed_period: Main diary 19 May–13 July 1838; return to Simla afterward. Particular royal routines and named events belong to this late reign.

passages.account: Villages on the journey are described with mud turrets, musket loopholes and shallow dry ditches.
passages.use: Vernacular defence reference to compare with earlier evidence; the author's generalization is not a census.

passages.account: An open-front scarlet-and-gold shawl tent, sword and shield beside the pillow, and a saddled horse ready outside.
passages.use: A later-reign night-to-dawn camp composition.

passages.account: Golden howdahs, guards in mail and quilted silk, and Suchet Singh's helmet, mail fringe, shawls, breastplates and shield.
passages.use: Elite equipment and costume variants, not ordinary cavalry's universal equipment.

passages.account: Visitors approach through guards, dismount, and reach a court with golden chairs, carpets and canopy; Ranjit wears simple white while chiefs sit on the floor.
passages.use: Later court choreography and contrasting status.

passages.account: Pack elephants carry shelter and cooking gear; a grove becomes a breakfast camp. Sewn fresh-leaf vessels hold food and liquid.
passages.use: Tent raising, transport loads, food service and conversation during adult Ranjit's excursions.

passages.account: A 30 June outing with Sher Singh reports boar, deer, black partridges and hares, with withy snares placed in boar runs.
passages.use: A specific hunt account and habitat lead; catch totals are not regional wildlife abundance.

passages.account: Wet tents become difficult to transport; later an overloaded open boat reaches the opposite bank far below its usual landing.
passages.use: Rain, baggage weight, current and displaced landings. Verify river identification before fixing this route on the map.

sources.geographic_note: The return narrative calls the crossing Ravee after Amritsar on the way to Ludhiana; retain that wording as a source claim, not a resolved map coordinate.
sources.wildlife_note: The tiger total at printed 114 / PDF 146 concerns Osborne's previous Terai and Dehra Dun hunt, not Punjab.

sources.title: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
sources.author: L. S. Buxi
sources.publisher: Publications Division, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Government of India, New Delhi
sources.kind: Modern popular biography with celebratory interpretation and an explicit popular-legends chapter

passages.account: Charat Singh moves from farming into horse trading after a mahatma's blessing.
passages.use: A horse-market journey that retains the blessing and introduces followers and alliances.

passages.account: A proposed Budh Singh name gives way to Ranjit following Maha Singh's Rasoolgarh victory.
passages.use: A campaign messenger and household naming scene; retain Rasoolgarh as this account's place name.

passages.account: Raj Kaur fears Lakhpat Rai's increasing power. The text presents and disputes allegations about her later death.
passages.use: Competing reports and protective political motives as well as darker traditions.

passages.account: Ranjit approaches Shah Zaman's walls and repeats a challenge on three days.
passages.use: Repeated reconnaissance, voiced challenge and withdrawal.

passages.account: Secret contact with Lahore residents, a night operation led by Sada Kaur, and orders protecting residents accompany entry on 7 July 1799 in this telling.
passages.use: Household contacts, coordinated gates and street-level discipline; printed quotation marks do not authenticate verbatim dialogue.

passages.account: An adolescent barehanded lion-killing story at Gujranwala is linked to Sheranwala Bagh.
passages.use: Retain as a fully stageable heroic tradition, with its status recorded internally.

passages.account: Stories include the soot-covered griddle exchanged for gold, carrying an old woman's grain, the berry-throwing boy, a clown's reprieve, repartee and the painter receiving a camel.
passages.use: Compact street encounters and character scenes for adult Ranjit, each retained as a popular legend.

sources.title: Maharaja Ranjit Singh: First Death Centenary Memorial
sources.kind: Multi-author historical memorial collection; claims must retain their chapter author and cited evidence

passages.account: The chapter combines intensive river-side cultivation, inundation canals and water lifting with thorny, pastoral Bar tracts west of Lahore and cattle/ghee livelihoods.
passages.use: A mosaic of cultivated settlements, grazing and scrub; not a uniformly uncultivated Punjab. Some agricultural evidence cited is from 1852 and later publications.

passages.account: The illustration is explicitly labelled Punjab 1839 and Intensive Cultivation.
passages.use: A later spatial reference, not a surveyed 1792 land-cover layer.

passages.account: The irrigation chapter describes an older Hasli canal, reconstruction and an Amritsar branch, as well as seasonal inundation channels.
passages.use: Pre-colonial water infrastructure, maintenance and disputes. The chapter's first-ruler assertion should not override its own acknowledgement of earlier canals.

passages.account: The chapter describes taqavi loans for wells, different crops and government regulation and maintenance of canals; many operate April–September.
passages.use: Later-empire water work and household obligations. Do not import this whole administration into childhood 1792.

passages.account: Wells offer an alternative when seasonal canals fail. Breaches can deprive downstream fields and produce crop-remission claims.
passages.use: A later-empire repair, water-access and compensation sequence; not an automatic 1792 rule.

passages.account: The chapter distinguishes actual produce division at the threshing floor, standing-crop estimates and cash, area, plough or well-based arrangements. Collection passes through village officials and the kardar.
passages.use: Harvest work, measurements, grain transport and disputed estimates. Preserve local variation rather than one universal tax rate.

passages.account: Kardars combine revenue and other administrative functions. Village panchayats hear disputes, with some unresolved matters reaching a kardar.
passages.use: Witness gathering, village arbitration and escalation for a later locally dated dispute.

passages.account: The essay discusses toll barriers, caravan conductors handling duties and merchants changing routes in response to excessive charges.
passages.use: A passage negotiation or longer detour for travelling parties after checking the specific route's date.

sources.source_relationship: A selective, sympathetic multi-author memorial. The bibliography begins at printed 257 / PDF 303 and includes early narratives and manuscripts alongside later settlement literature; a cited source is not necessarily contemporary with Ranjit.

sources.title: The Real Ranjit Singh: An Account based on the Archive of Fakir Family
sources.author: H. S. Virk
sources.kind: Short review or essay about Fakir Syed Waheed-ud-Din's book, not the book or the underlying Fakir archive
sources.identity_locator: Title and H. S. Virk byline in converted Word text
sources.read_method: Read legacy Word document through LibreOffice plain-text conversion; no reliable printed page locators assigned.

passages.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The author writes' and its four-item list
passages.account: The review relates a holy voice at the Lahore conquest setting duties of prayer, avoiding the Mughal throne, equal treatment and friendship with the Fakir family.
passages.use: A spiritual-political story or remembered counsel; retain the review-to-book-to-family-archive source chain.

passages.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Historians have not done justice'
passages.account: The review emphasizes Sada Kaur's rallying speech, Ranjit's challenge to Shah Zaman and her later conflict with Ranjit.
passages.use: Competing memories of who enabled his rise; quoted speech remains attributed through the review.

passages.locator: Paragraphs beginning 'Following the second commandment' and 'He had a keen sense'
passages.account: Simple personal attire and posture are contrasted with elaborate courtiers and surroundings.
passages.use: Adult court composition and dialogue. Absolutes such as never using emblems should not suppress contrary portrayals.

claims.value: Maha dies in 1792; child successor approximately twelve
Ranjit seven at father's death and eight on succession
1773, inferred from the 1774 marriage described as the following year
1767, attributed there to the Gujranwala gazetteer

variants.note: Date individual textual layers cautiously; an 1815 witness to chapter 1 is not a date certificate for every chapter.

existing_sequence_hooks.proposed_action: Choose and pack visible gifts within a household's means; reveal status and competing expectations in clothing and equipment.
Build or inspect a shared perimeter, carry tools, and negotiate watch assignments before the dispute over credit.
Give the warning and escort route distinct dwelling, kitchen, reception and stable spaces.
Develop mare handling and a household rest stop, keeping legendary biography and designed errands distinct internally.
Prepare and share a scarce meal through physical tasks before deciding what help to request or offer.
Enrich the later dawn storytelling frame without replacing the existing Bahrwal miracle or backdating this text to the legend.
